set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 52-year-old man becomes ill over 4 days with a temperature of 40.1 °C (104.2 °F), shaking chills and confusion. He looks toxic, a new loud regurgitant murmur is heard, and painless hemorrhagic macules appear on his soles, which are Janeway lesions (painless, nontender spots). Which form of infective endocarditis fits his course?
opts: Subacute disease is indolent: lower fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks or months, slow structural damage and rare metastasis.
Libman-Sacks endocarditis is the non-infective lesion of systemic lupus erythematosus; it does not cause high fever, toxicity and septic emboli.
Device endocarditis means vegetation on a pacemaker or defibrillator, and no device is described; his 4-day toxic course is the acute form.

Correct. Acute endocarditis is a hectically febrile illness from a virulent, invasive organism: rapid onset over 3-10 days, high fevers, systemic toxicity, rapid valve damage and seeding of extracardiac sites such as the skin.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 76-year-old woman had a mechanical mitral valve placed 4 years ago. She has 5 weeks of low-grade fever and fatigue, and blood cultures are pending. Which organism is most likely in her prosthetic valve infection?
opts: Correct. Late prosthetic valve endocarditis is caused by viridans streptococci, while early infection (around surgery) is caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus.
Staphylococcus epidermidis is the classic early prosthetic valve organism; 4 years out, viridans streptococci are expected.
Candida causes fungal endocarditis, mostly with immunocompromise or central lines; the late prosthetic valve organism is viridans streptococci.
Gram-negative bacilli are uncommon causes of endocarditis. Late prosthetic valve infection is viridans streptococcal.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 71-year-old man had his aortic valve replaced 6 weeks ago. He now has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F) and a new regurgitant murmur, and transesophageal imaging shows a vegetation on the prosthesis. Which organisms are most likely?
opts: Viridans streptococci cause late prosthetic valve endocarditis; at 6 weeks the organisms are staphylococci.
Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract; early prosthetic valve infection is staphylococcal.
The upper-airway HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms are not the early prosthetic valve organisms; staphylococci are.

Correct. Early prosthetic valve endocarditis is caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis) and Staphylococcus aureus, skin organisms introduced around the time of surgery.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 58-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve has a fever of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F) and conjunctival petechiae (pinpoint hemorrhages on the conjunctiva). No blood cultures or echocardiogram have been done yet. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Nothing here excludes endocarditis: a prosthetic valve, fever and conjunctival hemorrhages are three minor criteria, which make it possible.
Fever, the prosthetic valve and the conjunctival hemorrhages are each a minor criterion: three in all.
Correct. He has three minor criteria: a predisposing heart condition (prosthetic valve), fever, and a vascular phenomenon (conjunctival hemorrhages). Three minor criteria make endocarditis possible.
Definite needs two major, one major and three minor, or five minor criteria. Three minor criteria only reach possible.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: A 58-year-old woman with previous infective endocarditis needs a root canal. She developed hives (urticaria) after amoxicillin years ago and can take pills. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Cephalosporins should not be used after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria with penicillin, and she had hives.
ruled out by a stated finding
Amoxicillin is a penicillin and caused her hives, so it is avoided; a macrolide such as azithromycin is used instead.
ruled out by a stated finding
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.
Correct. A penicillin-allergic patient who can take oral medication gets azithromycin or clarithromycin, or doxycycline; cephalexin is avoided after urticaria to penicillin.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 45-year-old woman has 2 months of fever, weight loss and fatigue. A new murmur with a tumor plop (a low-pitched early diastolic sound) is heard, and three sets of blood cultures drawn before any antibiotics are negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Polymyalgia rheumatica causes myalgia and raised inflammatory markers, not a new murmur with a tumor plop.
Lyme disease causes fever and, rarely, myocarditis; it does not produce a tumor plop.
Correct. Atrial myxoma mimics endocarditis with fever and a new murmur, a tumor plop or mid-diastolic rumble, but it is a tumor and the cultures stay negative.
Subacute endocarditis usually grows an organism in cultures drawn before antibiotics, and a tumor plop is the sign of a cardiac tumor.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 61-year-old woman with mitral valve endocarditis develops worsening breathlessness, crackles and a new loud regurgitant murmur on day 3 of appropriate antibiotics. Echocardiography shows a ruptured chord with severe regurgitation. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the most common indication for surgery, and cardiothoracic surgery evaluates the need for surgery.
Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs; it does not address valve failure.
Palliative care may join a multidisciplinary plan, but heart failure from valve dysfunction calls for surgical evaluation.
This is a hospital problem needing urgent surgical evaluation, not an outpatient visit.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 57-year-old man with aortic valve endocarditis develops sharp chest pain and a scratchy friction rub on day 5 of treatment. Imaging shows infection spreading beyond the valve ring. Which process explains the new pericardial findings?
opts: Septal extension interrupts the conduction system; pericarditis follows extension into the epicardium.
Septic emboli to the coronary arteries
Coronary emboli could cause infarction, not a friction rub from spread of the abscess. Epicardial extension causes pericarditis.
Drug-induced lupus is not the mechanism. The abscess has spread into the epicardium, causing pericarditis.
Correct. A perivalvular abscess that extends into the epicardium causes pericarditis; extension into the upper ventricular septum would instead interrupt conduction.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: A 75-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve needs a dental extraction. He had a mild delayed rash (no hives, swelling or anaphylaxis) with penicillin and cannot take oral medication. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.

Correct. Penicillin-allergic patients unable to take oral medication receive cefazolin or ceftriaxone intramuscularly or intravenously, provided there is no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.
Ampicillin is a penicillin; the injectable penicillin is for patients without penicillin allergy.
ruled out by a stated finding
Azithromycin is an oral option, and he cannot take oral medication; cefazolin or ceftriaxone by injection fits.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 67-year-old woman has had 2 months of low-grade fevers to 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), fatigue and a 4-kilogram weight loss. She had a tooth extracted 10 weeks ago. A new apical systolic murmur is heard, and splinter hemorrhages (thin dark lines under the nail plates) are seen on two fingers. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. An indolent course with lower fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks to months, a new murmur, splinter hemorrhages and a dental source fits subacute endocarditis, classically from viridans streptococci.
Tuberculosis causes fever, night sweats and weight loss, but not a new murmur with splinter hemorrhages after dental work.
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes myalgia with high inflammatory markers; it does not produce a new murmur or splinter hemorrhages.
Acute disease is abrupt and toxic over 3-10 days with high fevers. Two months of low-grade fever and weight loss is subacute.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 77-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve has endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. His son asks how serious this organism is. Which statement is most accurate?
opts: A relatively good prognosis belongs to viridans streptococci treated before complications, not Staphylococcus aureus.
Prosthetic valve staphylococcal infection is severe; surgery is evaluated by cardiothoracic surgery when indicated.
Therapy alone runs weeks (typically 4-6 from the first negative culture), and the infection is the most lethal kind.
It is the most lethal cause
Correct. Staphylococcus aureus is the most lethal organism in endocarditis, with mortality highest in prosthetic valve endocarditis (about 50%).

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set1.q: An 8-year-old with endocarditis has a sudden fulminant illness with high spiking fevers, unlike the usual slow course in children. Which organisms does this presentation suggest?
opts: Fungal disease is tied to neonatal central lines; fulminant fevers suggest pneumococcus or Staphylococcus aureus.
Correct. A fulminant presentation with high spiking fevers suggests Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus, while most children have an indolent course.
Viridans streptococci cause the usual indolent pediatric course, not a fulminant one.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci are tied to prosthetic material and lines, not fulminant spiking fevers.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 74-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve placed 3 years ago has endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic valve infection adds rifampin and gentamicin to the antistaphylococcal drug, which is vancomycin when the strain is methicillin-resistant.
Nafcillin replaces vancomycin only when the strain is methicillin-susceptible; this strain is resistant.
ruled out by a stated finding
Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is an empiric native valve regimen; prosthetic staphylococcal infection adds rifampin and gentamicin.
Penicillin G with gentamicin is a viridans streptococcal regimen and does not treat methicillin-resistant staphylococci.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 59-year-old man is on day 6 of antibiotics for aortic valve endocarditis. He still has fevers, and today's electrocardiogram shows a new conduction block not present on admission. Which complication best explains the new conduction abnormality?
opts: Correct. When infection extends beyond the leaflets into the myocardium as a perivalvular abscess and reaches the upper ventricular septum, it interrupts the conduction system.
Septic emboli lodge in organs such as the lung, spleen and kidney; they do not explain a new conduction block, which points to a septal abscess.
Extension into the epicardium causes pericarditis. Conduction block follows extension into the upper ventricular septum.
Chordal rupture causes a new regurgitant murmur and heart failure, not a conduction block.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 55-year-old man has 3 days of fever to 40.0 °C (104.0 °F), rigors and a new murmur, and he looks toxic. Which organism is a classic cause of this tempo of infective endocarditis?
opts: Viridans streptococci cause subacute disease with low fevers over weeks, not a toxic course over 3 days.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci are listed with the subacute organisms and with early prosthetic valve infection; a classic acute organism is Staphylococcus aureus.
The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group causes subacute endocarditis, not the acute toxic form.
Correct. An abrupt, toxic, high-fever course is acute endocarditis, caused by virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and beta-hemolytic streptococci.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 65-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve has a fever of 38.7 °C (101.7 °F). Three blood cultures grow viridans streptococci, and a transesophageal echocardiogram shows new partial dehiscence of the prosthesis. How many major Duke criteria does he meet?
opts: Typical organisms in separate cultures and new prosthetic dehiscence are both major criteria.
Both the cultures and the echocardiographic dehiscence are major criteria, so he meets two.
Correct. A typical organism in separate cultures is one major criterion, and new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve on echocardiogram is the second; two major criteria make the case definite.
There are only two major criteria (blood culture and endocardial involvement); he meets both.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 47-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F) and Janeway lesions (painless hemorrhagic macules) on the soles of both feet. Blood cultures are pending. Under the modified Duke criteria, which category do the Janeway lesions fall into?
opts: Microbiologic evidence is a culture or serologic finding; the cultures here are still pending.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Janeway lesions are a vascular (embolic) phenomenon, a minor criterion with major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage and conjunctival hemorrhages.
Immunologic phenomena are glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor. Painless Janeway lesions are vascular.
Major endocardial evidence comes from echocardiography or new valvular regurgitation, not from skin lesions.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 57-year-old man with native valve endocarditis is improving on day 4 of intravenous antibiotics and asks whether he can switch to pills so he can go home sooner. Which reply is most accurate?
opts: Stopping early leaves bacteria alive in the vegetation; therapy is prolonged for weeks.
Stop when the fever is gone
Defervescence does not end therapy; the course is bactericidal, parenteral and runs 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture.
Correct. Antibiotics for endocarditis should be given parenterally and must be bactericidal and prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture; on day 4 the course has barely begun.
Pills work just as well now
On day 4 the standard is still parenteral therapy; endocarditis antibiotics are given parenterally, and an early switch to pills is not the approach.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set1.q: A 12-year-old had a ventricular septal defect closed with a prosthetic patch 4 months ago and is now scheduled for a dental extraction. Which is the most appropriate step regarding endocarditis?
opts: Delay is not the recommendation; a prophylactic dose before the extraction is, during the 6-month high-risk window.
Prophylaxis is given before the procedure so the drug is circulating during the bacteremia.
Correct. The first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material or a device is a high-risk period, and extraction manipulates the gums, so prophylaxis is given.
Within 6 months of repair with prosthetic material, the child is high risk and prophylaxis is indicated.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set1.q: A 17-year-old who injects drugs has fever, rigors and a tricuspid valve vegetation. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Candida is tied to neonatal catheters and hyperalimentation, not adolescent injection drug use.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci follow prosthetic material or recent surgery; injection drug use brings Staphylococcus aureus.
Correct. Adolescents increasingly resemble adults, including injection drug use-associated Staphylococcus aureus disease, which dominates tricuspid infection.
Viridans streptococci lead in younger children with congenital heart disease; injection drug use points to Staphylococcus aureus.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 38-year-old man who injects drugs has finished a course of intravenous antibiotics for tricuspid valve endocarditis and is preparing for discharge. He says he wants help to stay safe. Which consultation should be arranged?
opts: Renal function is monitored during antibiotics, but harm reduction for injection drug use is addiction medicine's role.
Correct. Addiction medicine is consulted for harm reduction in people who inject drugs, part of the multidisciplinary care with infectious disease and cardiothoracic surgery.
Dermatology has no listed role; harm reduction for injection drug use comes from addiction medicine.
Ophthalmology is not the consult for his drug use. Addiction medicine provides harm reduction.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 31-year-old man who injects drugs has tricuspid valve endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. He has no penicillin allergy. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus is treated with nafcillin or oxacillin, or cefazolin; vancomycin is the drug for methicillin-resistant strains and only an alternative for susceptible ones.
Vancomycin or daptomycin is the regimen for methicillin-resistant strains; with a susceptible strain and no penicillin allergy, nafcillin or oxacillin is preferred over vancomycin.
ruled out by a stated finding
Penicillin G with gentamicin is a viridans streptococcal regimen, not therapy for Staphylococcus aureus.
This is not an endocarditis regimen for Staphylococcus aureus; nafcillin or oxacillin is.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 64-year-old woman with mitral valve endocarditis has 2 days of worsening breathlessness and orthopnea (breathlessness when lying flat). A new, loud regurgitant murmur is heard and crackles fill both lung bases. Which mechanism explains her heart failure?
opts: Fever does not cause the heart failure described. Destroyed valve function, with a new regurgitant murmur, is the mechanism.
Intravenous antibiotics are not the mechanism given; the new regurgitant murmur points to valvular dysfunction.
Pericardial constriction is a separate disease. Endocarditis causes heart failure through valvular dysfunction.
Correct. Congestive heart failure in infective endocarditis is due to valvular dysfunction, here from leaflet damage or chordal rupture, and it is the most common indication for surgery.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: A 63-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve is having a tooth extracted tomorrow. He has no drug allergies and takes pills without difficulty. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.
A prosthetic valve is a high-risk condition, and extraction manipulates gums and roots, so prophylaxis is indicated.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. A high-risk patient (prosthetic valve) having an extraction gets a single dose of oral amoxicillin 30-60 minutes before the procedure, targeting viridans streptococci.
Prophylaxis is a single dose given before the procedure, not a week of antibiotics afterward.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 66-year-old woman in urgent care has a fever, a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages (dark lines under the nail plates). Before transfer, a colleague proposes giving a dose of ceftriaxone right away. Which action should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Empiric therapy is started only after blood cultures have been drawn; antibiotics given first may sterilize the cultures and lose the organism.
Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites are exactly what she needs before any antibiotic.
Endocarditis is managed in hospital with parenteral antibiotics and close monitoring, so admission is appropriate.
Echocardiography is part of the workup, looking for vegetations; it should not be avoided.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 34-year-old man who injects heroin has 4 days of fever to 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), rigors and a cough. A new holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border, and he looks toxic. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pneumonia would not explain a new holosystolic murmur in a person who injects drugs; fever, rigors, cough and that murmur point to tricuspid valve endocarditis.
A mitral murmur is loudest at the apex, not the left lower sternal border, and in people who inject drugs the valve singled out is the tricuspid.
Pericarditis brings positional chest pain and a friction rub, not a new holosystolic murmur with rigors in a person who injects drugs.

Correct. In people who inject drugs the tricuspid valve is the valve singled out (Staphylococcus aureus causes 80-90% of those infections); cough is linked to this group, and a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border fits the tricuspid valve.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 46-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F) and Janeway lesions (painless macules) on his palms. A transesophageal echocardiogram shows an oscillating mass on the tricuspid valve. Blood cultures are still pending. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Pending cultures do not prevent classification; one major and three minor criteria already make it definite.

Correct. One major criterion (the oscillating mass on echocardiogram) plus three minor criteria (injection drug use as predisposition, fever, and Janeway lesions as a vascular phenomenon) make endocarditis definite.
One major plus one minor would be possible, but he has one major plus three minor criteria, which is definite.
An oscillating mass on the tricuspid valve is a major criterion; with three minor criteria it confirms endocarditis rather than excluding it.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 39-year-old woman who injects drugs has native valve endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Ampicillin with gentamicin is an enterococcal regimen and does not treat methicillin-resistant staphylococci.
Correct. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is treated with vancomycin or daptomycin, the key difference from susceptible strains being vancomycin in place of a penicillin.
Nafcillin and oxacillin treat methicillin-susceptible strains; resistant strains need vancomycin or daptomycin.
ruled out by a stated finding
Cefazolin treats methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus; it does not cover resistant strains.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with a history of infective endocarditis has a fever of 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), Janeway lesions (painless macules) on her soles and Osler nodes (painful nodules) on two finger pads. One of three blood cultures grows viridans streptococci, the other two are negative, and echocardiography is not yet available. How is her case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: A missing echocardiogram does not block classification; five minor criteria already make endocarditis definite.

Correct. She has five minor criteria: predisposition (previous endocarditis), fever, a vascular phenomenon (Janeway lesions), an immunologic phenomenon (Osler nodes) and microbiologic evidence (one positive culture that misses the major criterion). Five minor criteria make the case definite.
Possible is one major plus one minor, or three minor criteria. She has five minor criteria, which reaches definite without any major criterion.
Five minor criteria confirm endocarditis rather than exclude it; one positive culture that misses the major criterion still counts as a minor one.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A 52-year-old woman on long-term immunosuppression has endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow Candida. Which complication is most likely?
opts: Correct. In fungal endocarditis the most likely complication is embolism and occlusion of larger peripheral arteries from embolization.
Fungal endocarditis is difficult to cure with medications alone and is an indication for surgery.
Rheumatic carditis is an immune reaction to streptococci, not a complication of Candida endocarditis.
A pericardial knock belongs to constrictive pericarditis; fungal endocarditis embolizes to large arteries.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 41-year-old man who injects drugs is being treated for tricuspid valve endocarditis. On day 2 he develops a new cough, and chest imaging shows several new scattered lesions in both lungs. Which complication best explains these findings?
opts: Aspiration causes a dependent pneumonia, not scattered lesions in both lungs; septic pulmonary emboli are a listed embolic complication.
Correct. The lung is among the listed embolic complications of infective endocarditis, and septic pulmonary infarcts count as a vascular phenomenon under the modified Duke criteria.
Antibiotic lung toxicity is not the listed complication; the lung is an embolic site of endocarditis, and septic pulmonary infarcts are a vascular phenomenon.
Heart failure from valve dysfunction floods the lungs diffusely; it does not make scattered lesions. Septic emboli to the lung do.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with acute endocarditis asks why the team is so worried when she felt well a week ago. Which statement about untreated acute endocarditis is accurate?
opts: It can be fatal within weeks
Correct. Acute endocarditis rapidly damages cardiac structures and seeds extracardiac sites; if untreated, it progresses to death within weeks.
Acute endocarditis does not resolve on its own; untreated, it progresses to death within weeks.
Smoldering for months is the subacute form; acute disease is rapidly destructive.
It is mainly a lung infection
Acute disease damages the valves and seeds many extracardiac sites; lung emboli are only one of them.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 70-year-old man has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F). Two separate blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus, a transesophageal echocardiogram shows no vegetation, and he has no predisposing heart condition, no drug use and no skin, eye or kidney findings. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Correct. He has one major criterion (a typical organism, Staphylococcus aureus, in two separate cultures) and one minor criterion (fever), which makes endocarditis possible.
Definite would need a second major criterion, three minor criteria with the one major, or five minor. He has one major and one minor.
A normal transesophageal echocardiogram does not necessarily rule out endocarditis, and the two positive cultures still meet a major criterion.
Two separate cultures of Staphylococcus aureus meet the major blood culture criterion, and his fever is a minor criterion.

set2.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with previous infective endocarditis brings an old wallet card that lists clindamycin for her dental prophylaxis. She has a penicillin allergy. Which counseling point is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Clindamycin is no longer recommended for prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection; she should be given an alternative such as azithromycin.
The recommendation changed: clindamycin was dropped because of Clostridioides difficile risk.
Amoxicillin is a penicillin and is avoided in her penicillin allergy; azithromycin or clarithromycin can be used.
ruled out by a stated finding
Previous endocarditis remains a high-risk condition, so prophylaxis is still needed.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 63-year-old woman with native mitral valve endocarditis after dental work has blood cultures growing penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci. Which antibiotic is a directed choice?
opts: Daptomycin is an option for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, not the directed streptococcal choice.
Correct. Viridans streptococci are treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone, with or without gentamicin, or vancomycin if penicillin cannot be used.
Nafcillin and oxacillin are antistaphylococcal penicillins for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus.
Rifampin and gentamicin are add-ons for staphylococcal prosthetic valve infection, not the streptococcal backbone.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set2.q: A 9-year-old with unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is scheduled for a tonsillectomy. Which is the most appropriate step regarding endocarditis?
opts: Prophylaxis is given before the procedure so the drug is circulating when bacteremia occurs.
Surgery need not be canceled; a single prophylactic dose before the tonsillectomy is the recommended approach.

Correct. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is a high-risk pediatric condition, and tonsillectomy is an invasive respiratory procedure with mucosal incision, so prophylaxis is given beforehand.
Both the condition and the procedure qualify: high-risk heart disease plus incision of respiratory mucosa.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 61-year-old woman with a prosthetic mitral valve has a fever of 38.7 °C (101.7 °F) and Osler nodes (painful red nodules on the pads of her fingers). Under the modified Duke criteria, which category do the Osler nodes fall into?
opts: Her prosthetic valve is the predisposition; the Osler nodes themselves are an immunologic phenomenon.
The blood culture criterion needs cultures, not a skin finding. Osler nodes are a minor immunologic phenomenon.
Correct. Osler nodes are painful and immunologic; with glomerulonephritis, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor they make up the immunologic minor criterion.
Vascular phenomena include painless Janeway lesions and conjunctival hemorrhages; painful Osler nodes are immunologic.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 49-year-old woman has subacute endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow Eikenella corrodens, a member of the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Rifampin is an add-on for staphylococcal prosthetic valve infection, not therapy for Eikenella, which is ceftriaxone.
Correct. HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) endocarditis is treated with ceftriaxone, or ampicillin-sulbactam.
Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not the treatment for these gram-negative organisms.
Vancomycin covers gram-positive organisms; gram-negative Eikenella and its group are treated with ceftriaxone.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 73-year-old man who lives at home has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and a new murmur. He has had no recent hospital stay, procedure or urinary symptoms, and no primary source of infection is found. Two separate blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. How do these cultures count under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Blood cultures count on their own; echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement is the other, separate major criterion, not a condition for this one.
Correct. Community-acquired enterococci in the absence of a primary focus count as a typical organism, so growth from two separate blood cultures meets the major blood culture criterion.
A positive culture that misses the major criterion is minor microbiologic evidence, but community-acquired enterococci without a primary focus in two cultures meet the major one.
Single cultures of coagulase-negative staphylococci or diphtheroids are excluded as contaminants; enterococci in two separate cultures are a typical organism.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 59-year-old man with native aortic valve endocarditis and a large vegetation asks whether a blood thinner would prevent a stroke. He has no other reason for anticoagulation. Which choice should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Anticoagulation is not beneficial in patients with native valve infection (it is controversial with prosthetic valves), so it should not be started for this reason.
Bactericidal parenteral antibiotics are the backbone of treatment and should continue.
Close monitoring of labs and renal function is part of endocarditis management and should continue throughout therapy.
Infectious disease directs antibiotics and outpatient monitoring; consulting them is appropriate.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 62-year-old man with fever has four sets of blood cultures drawn. One set grows coagulase-negative staphylococci, and the other three are negative. How should this single positive culture be counted under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Correct. Single positive cultures for coagulase-negative staphylococci (and diphtheroids) are excluded from the microbiologic criterion because they are common culture contaminants.
As the major blood culture criterion
The major criterion needs a typical organism in two separate cultures or persistent bacteremia, not one culture of a common contaminant.
Vascular phenomena are embolic findings such as Janeway lesions, not culture results.
One culture of a common contaminant proves nothing; it is excluded from the criteria.

set2.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
set2.q: A 70-year-old woman with a prosthetic aortic valve is scheduled for a screening colonoscopy and has no active infection. She asks whether she needs antibiotics beforehand. Which advice is most accurate?
opts: Amoxicillin prophylaxis is for dental procedures that manipulate gums or roots, not colonoscopy.
Prophylaxis is never a week-long course, and colonoscopy does not need any prophylaxis without active infection.
Vancomycin is not a prophylaxis choice here, and colonoscopy does not call for prophylaxis.

Correct. Gastrointestinal and genitourinary procedures such as colonoscopy, upper endoscopy and cystoscopy do not require endocarditis prophylaxis, even in high-risk patients, absent active infection.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: An 83-year-old woman is ready for discharge on day 9 of a planned 6-week course of intravenous antibiotics for endocarditis. She is deconditioned and cannot yet walk safely on her own. Which part of the multidisciplinary plan addresses this?
opts: Deconditioning is not a surgical indication; surgery is for heart failure, abscess, persistent infection or fungi.
Antibiotics continue for the full course; rehabilitation addresses her mobility.
Correct. The multidisciplinary team plans disposition, including rehabilitation, while infectious disease continues antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring.
Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs, not deconditioning.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: A 44-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 38.8 °C (101.8 °F) and Roth spots (white-centered retinal hemorrhages) on fundoscopy, meeting three minor Duke criteria. He has received no antibiotics. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure him that it is not endocarditis
Three minor criteria make endocarditis possible, not excluded, so reassurance is wrong; blood cultures from separate sites come first.
Order a chest radiograph and discharge
A chest radiograph cannot show vegetations. He needs blood cultures and echocardiography, not discharge.
Draw blood cultures from separate sites
Correct. Blood cultures (three sets from separate sites) come before any antibiotic; a positive culture with a typical organism would add a major criterion and make the case definite.
Start oral amoxicillin and recheck later
Oral amoxicillin is dental prophylaxis, not treatment, and antibiotics before cultures can leave the cultures negative.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 70-year-old man has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and malaise that began a week after a dental extraction. A new murmur of mitral regurgitation is heard. Three sets of blood cultures are drawn. Which organism are they most likely to grow?
opts: Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract, not the mouth; an oral source after dental work brings viridans streptococci.
Candida causes fungal endocarditis in the immunocompromised and in patients with central lines, not subacute disease after a tooth extraction.
Correct. The oral cavity is the source of viridans streptococci, the classic cause of subacute endocarditis after dental procedures and the organism dental prophylaxis targets.
Staphylococcus aureus is a skin organism that causes acute, toxic disease; a smoldering course after dental work points to viridans streptococci.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 64-year-old man will finish 5 more weeks of intravenous antibiotics for endocarditis after discharge. Which consultant manages his antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring?
opts: Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs, not antibiotic monitoring.
Dermatology has no listed role in endocarditis antibiotic management; infectious disease directs the antibiotic plan.
Correct. Infectious disease manages antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring pending disposition, as part of the multidisciplinary team.
Cardiothoracic surgery evaluates surgery and anticoagulation needs, not the outpatient antibiotic plan.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 29-year-old woman who injects drugs has 5 days of high fever and rigors. Transthoracic imaging shows a large vegetation on the tricuspid valve, and three sets of blood cultures are drawn from separate sites. Which organism are the cultures most likely to grow?
opts: Viridans streptococci follow oral sources such as dental work. Injection through the skin introduces Staphylococcus aureus.
Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract. Tricuspid endocarditis in a person who injects drugs is Staphylococcus aureus in 80-90%.
Candida is a fungal cause linked to immunocompromise and central lines; the dominant organism in injection drug use is Staphylococcus aureus.
Correct. In people who inject drugs, Staphylococcus aureus causes more than 60% of all endocarditis and 80-90% of cases where the tricuspid valve is infected.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 28-year-old woman with a malar rash, painful joints and a positive antinuclear antibody test has a new murmur. She has no fever, repeated blood cultures are negative, and echocardiography shows small sterile-appearing valve vegetations. Which is the most likely cause of her valve lesion?
opts: Without fever and with repeatedly negative cultures, a lupus patient's valve lesion is far more likely non-infective Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
ruled out by a stated finding
Acute endocarditis is hectically febrile and toxic with positive cultures, which she lacks.
ruled out by a stated finding
No pacemaker or defibrillator is described; her lupus, absent fever and negative cultures point to a non-infective valve lesion.
Correct. Systemic lupus erythematosus may present with non-infective (Libman-Sacks) endocarditis, which mimics infective endocarditis in the autoimmune differential.

set2.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
set2.q: A 52-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve is booked for a diagnostic bronchoscopy. No biopsy or mucosal incision is planned. Which advice about endocarditis prophylaxis is most accurate?
opts: Plain bronchoscopy is on the list that does not need prophylaxis; only mucosal incision or biopsy changes that.
Prophylaxis is never a week-long course, and none is needed for this bronchoscopy.
Vancomycin is not the standard prophylaxis and none is needed for this bronchoscopy.
None is needed for this procedure
Correct. Bronchoscopy does not require prophylaxis unless it involves incision of the respiratory mucosa, such as a biopsy.

set2.q: An 85-year-old man with degenerative aortic valve disease presents with fever and a new murmur. His family is surprised that a heart infection could occur at his age. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Age raises the risk rather than lowering it: patients over 60 make up more than half of all cases.
Over-60s are over half of cases
Correct. Risk is increased among the elderly: patients over 60 account for more than 50% of cases, and degenerative valve disease is now a leading predisposing condition.
It occurs mainly in drug users
Injection drug use is one risk factor, but more than half of cases occur in people over 60.
Pediatric endocarditis has low incidence; most cases are in older adults, with over-60s more than half.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 66-year-old man with subacute endocarditis has a fundoscopic examination that shows Roth spots (white-centered retinal hemorrhages). What process causes these spots?
opts: Raised intracranial pressure swells the optic disc; it does not make white-centered hemorrhages.
Hypertension causes its own retinopathy. Roth spots reflect vasculitis of small retinal arteries in endocarditis.
Correct. Roth spots are white-centered hemorrhages from vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina, grouped with the immunologic phenomena in the Duke criteria.
Trauma and detachment are not the mechanism. Roth spots come from vasculitis of the small retinal arteries.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman has a fever, a new murmur and Janeway lesions (painless macules on her soles), and two blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Her transesophageal echocardiogram is read as normal. Which conclusion is correct?
opts: She has a skin infection instead
Janeway lesions are embolic (vascular) signs of endocarditis, not a skin infection, and they support the diagnosis.
Correct. A normal transesophageal echocardiogram does not necessarily rule out endocarditis; Staphylococcus aureus in two separate cultures still meets a major criterion.
Even a highly sensitive test can miss vegetations. A normal study does not necessarily rule out endocarditis.
Staphylococcus aureus in two separate cultures is a typical endocarditis organism, not contamination.
ruled out by a stated finding

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 63-year-old woman has been in the hospital for 9 days after hip surgery. She develops a new fever, and two sets of blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus; she has no indwelling catheter, and examination finds no wound or other source. Which diagnosis must be suspected?
opts: Two separate cultures growing Staphylococcus aureus are not contamination; Staphylococcus aureus is a typical endocarditis organism.
ruled out by a stated finding
Atelectasis does not cause bacteremia. Fever with positive cultures and no source raises health care-associated endocarditis.
Drug fever does not produce positive blood cultures. Unexplained bacteremia in a hospitalized patient raises health care-associated endocarditis.

Correct. Health care-associated endocarditis should be suspected in hospitalized patients who develop fevers and positive blood cultures without an apparent source; Staphylococcus aureus causes about half of these cases.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set2.q: A 7-year-old with congenital heart disease is admitted with viridans streptococcal endocarditis. Which approach to antibiotic therapy is most appropriate?
opts: Children receive intravenous, not intramuscular, therapy, and doses are weight-based rather than fixed adult doses.
Oral one-week therapy cannot sterilize a vegetation; therapy is prolonged and intravenous.
Pediatric endocarditis has substantial mortality; it is treated with prolonged intravenous antibiotics.
Correct. Pediatric therapy is essentially the same as adult: prolonged, bactericidal, parenteral (intravenous, not intramuscular), pathogen-directed and weight-based.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 69-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter for 2 days of new confusion. She has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), a new murmur and conjunctival petechiae (pinpoint hemorrhages on the conjunctiva). Brain imaging shows multiple small scattered lesions without a large stroke. Which mechanism best explains her confusion?
opts: No conduction block is described; scattered lesions with fever and a murmur point to septic emboli.
No sedating drug is described; fever, a murmur, petechiae and scattered brain lesions point to septic emboli from a vegetation.
Correct. Vegetations shower septic emboli into the systemic circulation; the brain is affected (ischemic stroke, abscess, hemorrhage, meningitis), producing neurologic deficits such as confusion.
Meningitis is one cerebral complication, but scattered small lesions with a new murmur and petechiae point to septic emboli from a vegetation.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set2.q: A 4-month-old with tachycardia, poor feeding, respiratory distress and hypotension is being worked up for sepsis. A new murmur is heard. Why must endocarditis be considered even though the presentation looks like sepsis?
opts: Classic peripheral stigmata are considerably less common in children, so their absence does not exclude endocarditis.
Arthralgias belong to the indolent course of older children, not to infants, who present like sepsis.
Sepsis is common in infants; the point is that infant endocarditis looks like sepsis, so a new murmur must prompt the search for it.

Correct. In neonates and infants endocarditis presents nonspecifically and is often indistinguishable from sepsis or heart failure: feeding difficulty, respiratory distress, tachycardia, hypotension and a new or changing murmur.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 72-year-old woman has 6 weeks of aching and stiffness in her shoulders and hips, fatigue and a low-grade fever. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are high, but no murmur is heard and three sets of blood cultures are negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Polymyalgia rheumatica sits in the differential of endocarditis because it causes myalgia with elevated inflammatory markers, but there is no murmur and cultures are negative.
Subacute endocarditis brings a new murmur and positive cultures in most patients; neither is present here.
ruled out by a stated finding
Atrial myxoma would give fever with a new murmur, such as a tumor plop; she has no murmur.
ruled out by a stated finding
Antiphospholipid syndrome mimics endocarditis through thromboemboli and valve disease, not girdle myalgia.

set2.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set2.q: A 71-year-old woman with a prosthetic mitral valve is having a gum biopsy. She is not allergic to penicillin, but she cannot swallow pills after a recent stroke. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: A prosthetic valve is high risk, and a biopsy perforates the oral mucosa, so prophylaxis is indicated.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. A patient without penicillin allergy who cannot take oral medication receives ampicillin intramuscularly or intravenously (or cefazolin or ceftriaxone) 30-60 minutes before.
She cannot take oral medication, so the oral amoxicillin standard is not possible; ampicillin by injection is used.
ruled out by a stated finding
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 79-year-old man has enterococcal endocarditis of the aortic valve after recurrent urinary infections. Which outcome is he at notable risk for?
opts: Lung emboli are not the outcome singled out for enterococci; antibiotic resistance makes them hard to treat, with valve replacement in about 30-40%.
Correct. Enterococcal endocarditis is difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance, and major complications with need for valve replacement occur in about 30-40%.
Enterococcal endocarditis does not cure itself; it is difficult to treat because of resistance.
Enterococci are not the low-risk organism; antibiotic resistance makes them hard to treat, with valve replacement in 30-40%.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: A 56-year-old man on chemotherapy has Candida endocarditis confirmed on blood cultures and echocardiography. Which referral is most appropriate in addition to infectious disease?
opts: Correct. Fungal infection is difficult to cure with medications alone and is an indication for surgery, so cardiothoracic surgery evaluates him.
Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs; he has fungal infection needing surgical evaluation instead.
Rehabilitation may come later, but fungal endocarditis needs surgical evaluation now.
Dermatology has no role in fungal valve infection; cardiothoracic surgery evaluates the need for an operation.
